title: Lab 01: Converting Vague Prompts into Scoped OSINT Requirements
objective: Transform a vague investigative request about `example.com` into three structured, answerable Intelligence Requirements (IRs) and map each step to the OSINT Cycle.
steps: Read the scenario prompt: 'Tell me everything publicly known about the domain example.com.'

Break that overly broad prompt into 3 bounded Intelligence Requirements: IR-1 (Registration & authoritative body via ICANN RDAP), IR-2 (Published DNS records A/AAAA/MX/TXT), and IR-3 (Historical archival footprint via Wayback Machine).
Open https://lookup.icann.org in a browser tab and look up `example.com`.
Record the authoritative IANA/ICANN status codes (`clientDeleteProhibited`, etc.) and registry organization in your lab notes.
Verify which phase of the OSINT Cycle corresponds to defining IR-1..IR-3 vs querying ICANN RDAP.
expectedOutcome: A written 3-row Collection Plan mapping each Intelligence Requirement to an authorized passive source and UTC timestamp.

selfCheck.prompt: Which phase of the OSINT Cycle comes FIRST before any data collection?
selfCheck.explanation: Planning & Direction always precedes Collection so you define lawful, specific Intelligence Requirements.

selfCheck.prompt: According to RFC 2606 and ICANN RDAP, which organization reserves `example.com` for documentation?
selfCheck.explanation: IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) reserves example.com, example.net, and example.org under RFC 2606.

title: Lab 02: Classifying Zero-Touch Passive vs Active Actions
objective: Audit ten common reconnaissance actions and classify which ones stay strictly inside the zero-touch passive boundary.
steps: Review these four actions against target `iana.org`: (A) Querying `https://crt.sh/?q=iana.org`, (B) Running `nmap -sS iana.org`, (C) Reading Wayback snapshots on `web.archive.org`, (D) Running `gobuster` directory brute-forcing.
Trace the network packet destination for each action: does your packet go to a public third-party archive (`crt.sh`, `archive.org`) or directly to `iana.org`?
Document why (B) and (D) cross into active reconnaissance and require explicit written Rules of Engagement (RoE).
expectedOutcome: Clear packet-destination classification table separating zero-touch passive lookups from active probing.

selfCheck.prompt: Querying crt.sh for a domain's TLS certificates sends packets to crt.sh rather than the target. Is this passive or active?
selfCheck.hint: Zero packets touch the target server.
selfCheck.explanation: Because your browser only queries the public Certificate Transparency database (crt.sh), zero packets touch the target.

selfCheck.prompt: What three-letter acronym stands for the written document defining authorized scope and permitted techniques?
selfCheck.explanation: Rules of Engagement (RoE) formally define scope, dates, allowed methods, and legal authorization.

title: Lab 03: Auditing Browser Footprint & Profile Compartmentalization
objective: Create a dedicated, clean browser profile for OSINT study and inspect what HTTP headers your browser sends to websites.
steps: Create a separate browser profile (e.g., Firefox Multi-Account Containers or a clean Chromium profile) with zero personal accounts logged in.
Open Developer Tools (F12 -> Network tab) and visit `https://www.iana.org/domains/reserved`.
Click the main document request and inspect Request Headers: note `User-Agent`, `Accept-Language`, and absence of personal session cookies.
Verify WebRTC leak settings (`media.peerconnection.enabled` in Firefox `about:config` when using a VPN) and document OPSEC findings.
expectedOutcome: Isolated study browser profile verified free of personal cookies, autofill data, and extension telemetry.

selfCheck.prompt: Which HTTP request header reveals your browser name and operating system to every site you visit?
selfCheck.explanation: The User-Agent header discloses browser engine, version, and host OS architecture.

selfCheck.prompt: Which browser real-time communication feature can leak local/ISP IP addresses even while using a VPN if unconfigured?
selfCheck.hint: Starts with Web and ends with RTC.
selfCheck.explanation: WebRTC STUN requests can expose underlying network interface IPs unless restricted.

title: Lab 04: Applying Proportionality & Data Minimization
objective: Evaluate three real-world research requests for proportionality, privacy law compliance, and anti-doxxing boundaries.
steps: Review Case 1: Checking whether a vendor domain was registered yesterday before wiring an invoice payment.
Review Case 2: Publishing a private citizen's residential address during an online dispute.
Apply Data Minimization and Public-Interest tests: confirm Case 1 is lawful fraud prevention using corporate/domain records, while Case 2 is unethical doxxing and must be refused.
Write a 4-point personal OSINT Code of Conduct in your study notes.
expectedOutcome: Completed ethical impact checklist distinguishing legitimate pattern analysis from prohibited doxxing.

selfCheck.prompt: What privacy principle states you should collect only the minimum data strictly required for a lawful objective?
selfCheck.explanation: Data minimization (core to GDPR and ethical OSINT) prevents hoarding unnecessary personal data.

selfCheck.prompt: What is the term for unethically publishing private residential or contact details to harass an individual?
selfCheck.explanation: Doxxing violates professional OSINT ethics and privacy statutes worldwide.

title: Lab 05: Inspecting Public DNS Records for example.com & iana.org
objective: Identify A, AAAA, MX, NS, and TXT records for reserved public domains using public DNS resolvers.
steps: Query public DNS records for `example.com` using Google Public DNS web resolver (`https://dns.google/query?name=example.com&type=A`) or `dig example.com ANY`.
Repeat for `AAAA` (IPv6), `NS` (authoritative nameservers), `MX` (mail servers), and `TXT` (SPF policy).
Notice `v=spf1 -all` in `example.com`'s TXT record and interpret what `-all` tells mail receivers (this domain sends zero legitimate email!).
expectedOutcome: Complete DNS table for `example.com` recording IPv4, IPv6, NS, MX, and SPF TXT values.

selfCheck.prompt: Which DNS record type maps a hostname to a 128-bit IPv6 address?
selfCheck.explanation: AAAA ('quad-A') records map domain names to 128-bit IPv6 addresses, whereas A records map to 32-bit IPv4.

selfCheck.prompt: In `v=spf1 -all`, which email authentication standard is defined inside this DNS TXT record?
selfCheck.explanation: Sender Policy Framework (SPF) specifies authorized sending servers; `-all` hard-fails all unauthorized spoofed mail.

title: Lab 06: Analyzing Crawler Directives & Cached Index Mechanics
objective: Understand how search engines obey `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml` using archived public snapshots.
steps: Open the Wayback Machine (`https://web.archive.org`) and view an archived copy of `https://www.wikipedia.org/robots.txt`.
Identify `User-agent:` blocks, `Disallow:` rules, and `Sitemap:` declarations.
Record why `robots.txt` is an indexing politeness standard (RFC 9309) rather than an access-control security boundary.
expectedOutcome: Annotated breakdown of `User-agent`, `Disallow`, and `Sitemap` directives from an archived `robots.txt`.

selfCheck.prompt: What root filename instructs search crawlers which URL paths not to index?
selfCheck.explanation: robots.txt (standardized in RFC 9309) provides crawler exclusion directives at the site root.

selfCheck.prompt: What XML file commonly referenced in robots.txt lists public URLs and lastmod timestamps for indexing?
selfCheck.explanation: sitemap.xml enumerates canonical public pages and update timestamps to aid search engine indexing.

title: Lab 07: Verifying File Signatures (Magic Bytes) & SHA-256 Integrity
objective: Create a local test file on your own computer, compute its SHA-256 digest, and inspect JPEG/PDF magic numbers in CyberChef.
steps: Open CyberChef (`https://gchq.github.io/CyberChef/`)—which runs 100% locally in your browser.
Load any personal test photo or create a tiny PNG/JPEG from scratch, then apply the 'Detect File Type' and 'To Hex' operations.
Verify the leading hexadecimal bytes: `FF D8 FF` for JPEG, `89 50 4E 47` for PNG, or `25 50 44 46` (`%PDF`) for PDF.
Add the 'SHA2' (256-bit) operation in CyberChef, record the 64-character hex hash, then change 1 single byte and observe the avalanche effect.
expectedOutcome: Verified hex magic signatures and SHA-256 before/after digests demonstrating tamper detection.

selfCheck.prompt: What are the first four hexadecimal characters (magic number) of a standard JPEG image?
selfCheck.explanation: Every standard JPEG stream begins with Start of Image (SOI) marker bytes FF D8 (followed by FF).

selfCheck.prompt: How many hexadecimal characters long is a SHA-256 hash digest?
selfCheck.hint: 256 bits divided by 4 bits per hex character.
selfCheck.explanation: 256 bits / 4 bits per hex digit = 64 hexadecimal characters.

title: Lab 08: Filtering Subdomain Lists Locally with Linux CLI Pipes
objective: Use `grep`, `sort`, `uniq`, and `wc` on a sample passive CT log export to deduplicate hostnames.
steps: Save a plain-text list of 20 sample `*.example.org` hostnames containing duplicates and wildcard `*.` prefixes into `ct_sample.txt`.
Run `cat ct_sample.txt | sed 's/^\*\.//' | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sort -u` to normalize case, strip wildcard prefixes, and deduplicate.
Pipe the output to `grep -E '(dev|staging|vpn)'` to isolate high-interest infrastructure naming patterns.
Count unique entries with `wc -l`.
expectedOutcome: Clean, lowercase, deduplicated hostname list produced purely with standard POSIX command-line tools.

selfCheck.prompt: Which flag on the Linux `sort` command outputs only unique (deduplicated) lines?
selfCheck.hint: Single dash followed by the first letter of unique.
selfCheck.explanation: `sort -u` sorts lines alphabetically and removes duplicates in a single pass.

selfCheck.prompt: Which Linux CLI utility inspects magic bytes to report a file's actual data type regardless of extension?
selfCheck.hint: Four-letter command literally named after what it inspects.
selfCheck.explanation: The POSIX `file` command checks magic byte signatures against libmagic definitions.

title: Lab 09: Crafting Precision Search Operators Across Official Docs
objective: Construct Boolean and field-restricted search queries (`site:`, `filetype:`, `intitle:`) targeting public standards bodies (`ietf.org`, `nist.gov`).
steps: Construct a query finding PDF publications on `csrc.nist.gov` mentioning 'threat intelligence': `site:csrc.nist.gov filetype:pdf "threat intelligence"`.
Construct a query finding RFC pages on `datatracker.ietf.org` with 'Certificate Transparency' in the HTML title: `site:datatracker.ietf.org intitle:"Certificate Transparency"`.
Test excluding noisy subdomains with the minus operator (`-site:mailarchive.ietf.org`) and compare result precision across Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo.
expectedOutcome: Three verified multi-operator queries returning high-signal primary technical documents.

selfCheck.prompt: Which search operator restricts results strictly to a specific domain or subdomain?
selfCheck.hint: Four letters followed by a colon.
selfCheck.explanation: `site:example.org` restricts search results to pages indexed under that domain.

selfCheck.prompt: Which search operator filters results by document extension such as pdf, xlsx, or docx?
selfCheck.explanation: `filetype:pdf` (or `ext:pdf`) restricts indexed documents by file format.

title: Lab 10: Querying Wayback Machine CDX Index for Historical Changes
objective: Retrieve historical snapshots and plain-text CDX capture metadata for `example.com` without touching the live server.
steps: Open `https://web.archive.org/web/*/example.com` and compare a 2005 capture of `example.com` with a 2024 capture.
Note how the authoritative explanation text and RFC references evolved over two decades.
Inspect the CDX API endpoint format: `https://web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=example.com&output=json&limit=5` to see `[urlkey, timestamp, original, mimetype, statuscode, digest, length]`.
Observe how identical `digest` hashes across dates prove a page did NOT change between two crawls.
expectedOutcome: Timeline log comparing historical `example.com` revisions and interpreting CDX digest fields.

selfCheck.prompt: What is the name of the Wayback Machine's index API (`.../cdx/search/cdx`) that returns tabular capture metadata?
selfCheck.hint: Three-letter acronym in the URL path.
selfCheck.explanation: The Capture Index (CDX) API returns structured capture timestamps, HTTP codes, and content hashes.

selfCheck.prompt: In a Wayback Machine snapshot URL (`.../web/20230501123000/...`), how many digits represent the YYYYMMDDHHMMSS timestamp?
selfCheck.explanation: Wayback timestamps use a 14-digit UTC format: YYYYMMDDHHMMSS.

title: Lab 11: Tracing IP Ownership Across ICANN RDAP & Regional Registries
objective: Trace `93.184.215.14` / reserved documentation netblocks (`192.0.2.0/24`) across ARIN/RIPE RDAP to distinguish domain registrars from IP hosting owners.
steps: Look up `iana.org` in `https://lookup.icann.org` to inspect domain-level registrar and nameserver records.
Look up RFC 5737 documentation block `192.0.2.1` (`TEST-NET-1`) in `https://search.arin.net`.
Contrast Domain Registration (ICANN/Registrar) vs IP Netblock Allocation (IANA -> RIR -> ISP/Cloud ASN).
expectedOutcome: Clear two-layer ownership diagram separating Domain Registrar metadata from RIR Netblock/ASN ownership.

selfCheck.prompt: Which modern HTTPS/JSON protocol has officially replaced legacy port-43 WHOIS at ICANN?
selfCheck.explanation: RDAP (Registration Data Access Protocol) delivers standardized JSON responses over HTTPS.

selfCheck.prompt: Which Regional Internet Registry (RIR) manages IP allocations for Europe and the Middle East?
selfCheck.explanation: RIPE NCC serves Europe, the Middle East, and parts of Central Asia.

title: Lab 12: Passive Subdomain Enumeration via Certificate Transparency (crt.sh)
objective: Query `crt.sh` using wildcard SQL `%` syntax and JSON output on `iana.org` to build a 100% passive subdomain inventory.
steps: Navigate to `https://crt.sh/?q=%25.iana.org` (`%.iana.org`) in your study browser.
Inspect the `Matching Identities` (Subject Alternative Names) and `Issuer Name` columns.
Append `&output=json` (`https://crt.sh/?q=%25.iana.org&output=json`) to view machine-readable JSON entries.
Record 5 unique `*.iana.org` subdomains discovered without sending a single DNS brute-force packet.
expectedOutcome: Deduplicated passive subdomain table with certificate validity dates and issuing CAs.

selfCheck.prompt: Which X.509 certificate extension field lists multiple subdomains covered by a single TLS certificate?
selfCheck.explanation: Subject Alternative Name (SAN) fields frequently reveal sibling domains and subdomains on shared certs.

selfCheck.prompt: What URL query parameter (`output=...`) tells crt.sh to return structured JSON data?
selfCheck.explanation: Appending `&output=json` to crt.sh queries returns structured JSON ideal for local CLI parsing.

title: Lab 13: Mapping ASN Prefixes & Historical DNS Without Active Scanning
objective: Inspect Autonomous System AS15133 / IANA ASNs in Hurricane Electric BGP Toolkit (`bgp.he.net`) to understand CDN vs dedicated IP hosting.
steps: Open `https://bgp.he.net` and search `iana.org`.
Inspect the `DNS`, `IP Info`, and `Prefixes v4 / v6` tabs for the returned ASN.
Determine why seeing 500 unrelated domains on a Cloudflare or Fastly CDN IP does NOT mean those 500 organizations own each other!
expectedOutcome: ASN correlation note explaining dedicated enterprise netblocks vs multi-tenant CDN/cloud reverse proxies.

selfCheck.prompt: What three-letter routing acronym identifies an organization's numbered network of IP prefixes (e.g., AS13335)?
selfCheck.explanation: An Autonomous System Number (ASN) uniquely identifies a BGP routing domain.

selfCheck.prompt: Does DNS wordlist brute-forcing (`gobuster dns` / `massdns`) qualify as Stage A passive OSINT? (Answer yes or no)
selfCheck.hint: Wordlist brute-forcing sends thousands of live queries.
selfCheck.explanation: No—DNS brute-forcing actively generates high-volume query traffic and is outside passive OSINT.

title: Lab 14: Writing Shodan & Censys Search Queries Safely
objective: Master Shodan and Censys search syntax (`org:`, `asn:`, `ssl.cert.subject.cn:`, `http.title:`) conceptually and passively.
steps: Review Shodan filter syntax documentation: `ssl.cert.subject.cn:"example.com"`, `port:443`, `org:"Internet Assigned Numbers Authority"`.
Compare equivalent Censys Search query syntax: `services.tls.certificates.leaf_data.names: "example.com"`.
Explain why searching `ssl.cert.subject.cn:` often uncovers origin servers even when a domain's public A record sits behind a CDN!
expectedOutcome: Cheat-sheet translating 5 defensive asset discovery questions into both Shodan and Censys passive queries.

selfCheck.prompt: In Shodan query syntax, which filter searches HTML `<title>` tags (`http.____`)?
selfCheck.explanation: `http.title:"Login"` filters pre-indexed HTTP banners by page title.

selfCheck.prompt: When you search Shodan's web database, are packets sent from your machine to the indexed servers? (Answer yes or no)
selfCheck.hint: You are only querying Shodan's search database.
selfCheck.explanation: No—querying Shodan's database only searches previously collected banners; never connect directly to discovered hosts.

title: Lab 15: Corroborating Public Handles & Avoiding False-Positive Collisions
objective: Evaluate username reuse across public platforms using corroborating pivot anchors (bio links, PGP keys, avatar hashes, join timelines).
steps: Examine a synthetic case of handle `@alex_sec` appearing on GitHub, Keybase, Mastodon, and a gaming forum.

Compare secondary anchors: GitHub links to personal blog `alex-sec.example` and lists PGP fingerprint `4F9A...`; Mastodon uses `rel="me"` verification back to `alex-sec.example`; the gaming forum account was registered in a different decade with conflicting language/timezone.
Document why `@alex_sec` on GitHub + Mastodon is corroborated, while the gaming forum handle is a username collision.
expectedOutcome: Corroboration matrix showing strong cryptographic/bidirectional links (`rel=me`, PGP) vs weak handle-only collisions.

selfCheck.prompt: Does an identical username alone on two websites prove both accounts belong to the same person? (Answer yes or no)
selfCheck.explanation: No—handle collisions are extremely common; independent corroborating anchors are mandatory.

selfCheck.prompt: Which HTML link attribute (`rel="__"`) is used on Mastodon and personal websites to prove bidirectional profile ownership?
selfCheck.explanation: Linking both ways with `rel="me"` cryptographically/structurally confirms the site owner controls the social profile.

title: Lab 16: Auditing Domain Anti-Spoofing (SPF/DMARC) & k-Anonymity Breach Checks
objective: Inspect `_dmarc` DNS TXT policies and understand how Have I Been Pwned protects privacy via k-anonymity.
steps: Query `_dmarc.ietf.org` TXT record via `dig TXT _dmarc.ietf.org` or MXToolbox.
Identify the `v=DMARC1; p=...; rua=...` tags (`p=none`, `p=quarantine`, or `p=reject`).
Review how HIBP's Pwned Passwords API sends only the first 5 characters of a SHA-1 hash prefix so the full secret never leaves the client.
expectedOutcome: Email posture scorecard explaining SPF + DKIM + DMARC `p=reject` and ethical breach notification rules.

selfCheck.prompt: Which DNS subdomain prefix (`_____`.domain.com) stores a domain's DMARC TXT policy?
selfCheck.hint: Starts with an underscore followed by dmarc.
selfCheck.explanation: DMARC policies are always published as TXT records at `_dmarc.<domain>`.

selfCheck.prompt: In a DMARC record, which policy value (`p=______`) instructs mail servers to outright block failing spoofed emails?
selfCheck.explanation: `p=reject` instructs receiving mail servers to block messages failing SPF and DKIM alignment.

title: Lab 17: Multi-Engine Reverse Image & Object-Crop Methodology
objective: Compare TinEye ('Sort by Oldest') vs Google Lens / Yandex region-cropping on public Wikimedia Commons architectural photos.
steps: Select a public-domain landmark photo from Wikimedia Commons where foreground pedestrians or text overlays partially obscure a building.
Run the full uncropped image in TinEye and sort by 'Oldest' to locate earliest indexed web appearances.
Crop tightly around ONLY the permanent architectural roofline/tower (excluding foreground noise) and compare landmark recognition results.
expectedOutcome: Comparison note documenting when to use exact-match fingerprinting (TinEye) vs semantic architectural cropping.

selfCheck.prompt: Which reverse image search engine lets you sort matches by 'Oldest' crawl date to find earliest publication?
selfCheck.explanation: TinEye indexes exact/near-exact image fingerprints and lets analysts sort by Oldest crawl date.

selfCheck.prompt: When reverse-searching a video clip, what extracted still images provide the sharpest visual search input?
selfCheck.explanation: Keyframes (I-frames) store complete uncompressed spatial frame data rather than motion deltas.

title: Lab 18: Auditing Social Media EXIF Stripping & C2PA Provenance
objective: Understand why most major social platforms strip EXIF GPS tags on upload and how C2PA Content Credentials work.
steps: Take a harmless photo of a desk mug on your own device and inspect its raw EXIF fields locally using ExifTool or CyberChef.
Compare those tags against an image downloaded from a major social network—observing stripped camera/GPS tags and re-encoded JPEG quantization tables.
Visit `https://contentcredentials.org/verify` to inspect a sample C2PA-signed photograph and examine its cryptographic manifest tree.
expectedOutcome: Verification checklist preventing false 'no EXIF = fake' conclusions while checking C2PA and visual consistency.

selfCheck.prompt: Does the absence of EXIF metadata on a social media image prove the image was manipulated? (Answer yes or no)
selfCheck.hint: Almost all social networks strip EXIF automatically for privacy and compression.
selfCheck.explanation: No—platforms routinely strip EXIF metadata during upload recompression.

selfCheck.prompt: What four-character coalition standard (`C___`) embeds cryptographically signed Content Credentials in media?
selfCheck.explanation: C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) defines signed provenance manifests.

title: Lab 19: Geospatial Feature Mining with OpenStreetMap Overpass Turbo
objective: Write an Overpass QL spatial proximity query to pinpoint an intersection from visual clues (e.g., a lighthouse within 300m of a railway).
steps: Suppose a public postcard shows a lighthouse (`man_made=lighthouse`) standing within 250 meters of a railway track (`railway=rail`) inside a coastal region.
Open `https://overpass-turbo.eu`, zoom to a sample coastal area, and build a query finding `node["man_made"="lighthouse"]` and `way["railway"="rail"](around:250)`.
Inspect the candidate pins on satellite view (`earth.google.com`) to verify roofline geometry and road angle.
expectedOutcome: Working Overpass QL snippet narrowing thousands of square kilometers down to a handful of verifiable coordinates.

selfCheck.prompt: Which Overpass QL filter (`(______:250)`) finds features within a specified radius in meters of another set?
selfCheck.explanation: The `(around:<meters>)` spatial filter in Overpass QL intersects nearby OSM features.

selfCheck.prompt: Which collaborative open-data map project provides the underlying database queried by Overpass Turbo?
selfCheck.explanation: Overpass Turbo queries the crowdsourced OpenStreetMap (OSM) global vector database.

title: Lab 20: Solar Azimuth Chronolocation & Stage A Capstone Prep
objective: Use `SunCalc.org` to calculate exact local capture time from shadow bearing and build a UTC-normalized timeline.
steps: Pick a known landmark coordinate—for example, the Greenwich Royal Observatory (`51.4769, -0.0005`) on `2026-06-21`.
Suppose a vertical flagpole casts a shadow pointing directly due East (compass azimuth `90°`), meaning the sun is due West (`270°`).
Open `https://www.suncalc.org/#/51.4769,-0.0005,17/2026.06.21/12:00/1/3` and drag the time slider until the solar azimuth reads `270°`.
Record both the local British Summer Time (BST) and normalized UTC timestamp.
expectedOutcome: Verified chronolocation calculation converting shadow direction -> solar azimuth -> exact UTC capture window.

selfCheck.prompt: If an object casts a shadow pointing at 90° (due East), what is the sun's compass azimuth in degrees?
selfCheck.hint: Add 180 degrees to the shadow's bearing.
selfCheck.explanation: Shadows always fall 180° opposite the light source: 90° + 180° = 270° (due West).

selfCheck.prompt: Which three-letter global time standard must professional OSINT timelines normalize timestamps to?
selfCheck.explanation: UTC eliminates daylight-saving and multi-timezone ambiguity across global investigations.

title: Lab 21: Mapping an Intrusion Advisory to the Diamond Model & Pyramid of Pain
objective: Extract IOCs and TTPs from a public CISA cybersecurity advisory and map them onto the four Diamond Model vertices.
steps: Read a public CISA advisory snippet describing a spear-phishing campaign using a typosquatted domain (`login-portal-update[.]example`), a known malware SHA-256 hash, and PowerShell scheduled-task persistence.
Classify each artifact on David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain (Hash -> IP -> Domain -> Network/Host Artifacts -> Tools -> TTPs).
Populate the four Diamond Model vertices: Adversary, Infrastructure, Capability, and Victim.
expectedOutcome: Structured Diamond Model graph and Pyramid of Pain prioritization table.

selfCheck.prompt: Which layer sits at the VERY TOP of David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain as the hardest for attackers to change?
selfCheck.hint: Three-letter plural acronym: Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures.
selfCheck.explanation: TTPs (adversary behaviors) sit at the apex of the Pyramid of Pain; hashes sit at the bottom.

selfCheck.prompt: In the Diamond Model, domains, C2 IPs, and TLS certificates belong to which vertex?
selfCheck.explanation: The Infrastructure vertex holds network delivery and C2 assets—primary OSINT pivot territory.

title: Lab 22: Defensive Exposure Audit Mapped to MITRE ATT&CK TA0043
objective: Map passive OSINT findings (CT logs, PDF author leaks, job-post stack disclosures) to MITRE ATT&CK Reconnaissance technique IDs.
steps: Open `https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0043/`.

Match three findings to exact sub-techniques: (1) Harvesting subdomains from CT logs -> `T1596.003` (Search Open Technical Databases: Digital Certificates); (2) Inferring SIEM vendor from public job postings -> `T1591` / `T1592`; (3) Extracting employee emails from public PDFs -> `T1589.002`.
Write one defensive mitigation (e.g., Pre-compromise OPSEC / metadata scrubbing) for each technique.
expectedOutcome: MITRE ATT&CK Navigator-ready technique mapping table with defensive mitigations.

selfCheck.prompt: What is the official MITRE ATT&CK Tactic ID (`TA____`) for Reconnaissance?
selfCheck.explanation: TA0043 is the MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise tactic identifier for Reconnaissance.

selfCheck.prompt: Under T1596 (Search Open Technical Databases), does querying Certificate Transparency logs map to `T1596.003` Digital Certificates? (Answer yes or no)
selfCheck.explanation: Yes—T1596.003 specifically covers adversary and defender lookups of public digital certificate logs.

title: Lab 23: Defanging IOCs & Packaging STIX 2.1 Indicators Under TLP 2.0
objective: Safely defang live-formatted malicious indicators in CyberChef and assign proper FIRST TLP 2.0 sharing labels.
steps: Take sample indicator `https://auth-verify.bad-example.org/login` and apply CyberChef's 'Defang URL' recipe (`hxxps://auth-verify[.]bad-example[.]org/login`).
Review FIRST TLP 2.0 designations (`TLP:RED`, `TLP:AMBER+STRICT`, `TLP:AMBER`, `TLP:GREEN`, `TLP:CLEAR`).
Inspect a JSON STIX 2.1 `indicator` object containing `pattern: "[domain-name:value = 'auth-verify.bad-example.org']"`.
expectedOutcome: Sanitized defanged IOC table with valid STIX 2.1 pattern syntax and TLP 2.0 sharing header.

selfCheck.prompt: When defanging an `https://` URL, what five-letter string replaces `https`?
selfCheck.explanation: `hxxps` prevents chat clients, ticketing tools, and email readers from auto-linking malicious URLs.

selfCheck.prompt: In FIRST TLP 2.0, which designation replaced legacy `TLP:WHITE` for unrestricted public sharing (`TLP:_____`)?
selfCheck.explanation: TLP 2.0 replaced TLP:WHITE with TLP:CLEAR for publicly shareable intelligence.

title: Lab 24: SOC L1 Alert Triage & External OSINT Enrichment
objective: Triage three synthetic SIEM firewall/proxy alerts by enriching external IPs and domains with GreyNoise, RDAP age, and ASN context.
steps: Inspect Alert A: Inbound TCP/443 scan from a documented Censys scanner subnet -> Verify benign `RIOT`/scanner tag in GreyNoise -> Close as benign background scan.
Inspect Alert B: Outbound DNS/HTTPS connection from workstation `WS-042` to a domain registered 18 hours ago on a high-abuse bullet-proof ASN.
Write a concise SOC L1 escalation note for Alert B citing domain age (<24h), ASN context, and passive DNS lack of prior history.
expectedOutcome: Completed SOC L1 triage ticket separating false positives from newly registered C2 communication.

selfCheck.prompt: Is a domain registered less than 24 hours ago (Newly Registered Domain / NRD) generally higher or lower risk in outbound enterprise proxy logs?
selfCheck.hint: Phishing and C2 domains are frequently spun up hours before use.
selfCheck.explanation: Newly Registered Domains (NRDs) carry significantly elevated phishing and C2 risk in corporate proxy traffic.

selfCheck.prompt: Which OSINT tool specializes in identifying mass internet background scanners to reduce SOC alert fatigue?
selfCheck.explanation: GreyNoise classifies mass internet-wide scanner traffic vs targeted attacks.

title: Lab 25: Pivoting Across Phishing Infrastructure Using Passive urlscan.io Data
objective: Use existing `urlscan.io` search queries (`page.domain:`, `hash:`, `cert.issuer:`) to pivot from one phishing URL to sibling domains safely.
steps: Open `https://urlscan.io/search/` (passive search interface—do NOT submit internal corporate URLs!).
Examine how `urlscan.io` indexes SHA-256 hashes of loaded logos, CSS files, and JavaScript bundles (`hash:<sha256>`).
Trace how reusing a single login-form JavaScript file allows defenders to find 20 newly deployed phishing domains across completely different TLDs.
expectedOutcome: Infrastructure pivot diagram showing Domain 1 -> Shared JS SHA-256 Hash -> Domains 2..N.

selfCheck.prompt: In urlscan.io search syntax, which prefix (`____:<sha256>`) finds all scanned pages loading an identical resource file?
selfCheck.explanation: Searching `hash:<sha256>` on urlscan.io pivots across every archived page serving that exact image, CSS, or script.

selfCheck.prompt: Should a SOC analyst submit a confidential internal password-reset link containing a live user token to a public urlscan.io scan? (Answer yes or no)
selfCheck.hint: Public scans are visible to everyone on the internet!
selfCheck.explanation: Never—public sandbox submissions publish screenshots, URLs, and DOM tokens to the public feed.

title: Lab 26: Risk-Based Vulnerability Triage with CVSS, EPSS & CISA KEV
objective: Prioritize three vulnerabilities by combining passive internet exposure with CVSS, EPSS probability, and CISA KEV active-exploitation status.
steps: Compare Vuln 1 (CVSS 9.8 on an offline internal test printer, EPSS 0.002, NOT in CISA KEV) vs Vuln 2 (CVSS 7.5 on an internet-facing VPN gateway visible in passive Censys records, EPSS 0.94, LISTED in CISA KEV).
Verify CISA KEV catalog fields (`cveID`, `vendorProject`, `dateAdded`, `dueDate`, `knownRansomwareCampaignUse`).
Justify why Vuln 2 receives emergency P1 remediation ahead of Vuln 1.
expectedOutcome: Evidence-based remediation matrix outperforming naive CVSS-only sorting.

selfCheck.prompt: Which U.S. agency maintains the authoritative Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog?
selfCheck.hint: Four-letter agency acronym starting with C.
selfCheck.explanation: CISA maintains the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

selfCheck.prompt: Which scoring system (`____`) estimates the 30-day probability (0 to 1) that a CVE will be exploited in the wild?
selfCheck.explanation: EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System, maintained by FIRST) predicts real-world exploitation likelihood.

title: Lab 27: Corporate Hierarchy & Sanctions Due Diligence via GLEIF & EDGAR
objective: Trace corporate parent-subsidiary trees using 20-character ISO 17442 LEI records and SEC EDGAR Exhibit 21 subsidiary filings.
steps: Open `https://search.gleif.org` and look up any major public multinational corporation.
Inspect 'Level 1 Data' (Who is who: legal name, registered address, registration authority ID) and 'Level 2 Data' (Who owns whom: direct and ultimate parent relationships).
Locate Exhibit 21 (`EX-21`) inside an annual `10-K` filing on SEC EDGAR (`sec.gov/edgar`) to see disclosed global subsidiaries.
expectedOutcome: Verified corporate ownership chart backed by GLEIF LEI codes and SEC Form 10-K Exhibit 21 citations.

selfCheck.prompt: How many alphanumeric characters make up a standard ISO 17442 Legal Entity Identifier (LEI)?
selfCheck.explanation: Every ISO 17442 LEI is an exact 20-character alphanumeric identifier.

selfCheck.prompt: Which annual SEC filing form (`__-_`) contains audited financials, risk factors, and Exhibit 21 subsidiary lists for U.S. public companies?
selfCheck.hint: Number 10 followed by a hyphen and a letter.
selfCheck.explanation: SEC Form 10-K is the comprehensive annual corporate disclosure filing.

title: Lab 28: Detecting Circular Reporting & Applying Two-Source Corroboration
objective: Audit a multi-article claim chain to detect circular reporting ('citogenesis') where three blogs cite the same unverified social post.
steps: Trace timestamps and hyperlinks across three news summaries claiming a corporate executive resigned.
Discover all three summaries trace back to a single 4-hour-old parody account handle with one swapped character (`homoglyph`).
Check official statutory officer filings and verified investor relations releases to refute the false claim safely without amplifying personal data.
expectedOutcome: Source provenance tree exposing single-origin circular reporting.

selfCheck.prompt: What flaw occurs when multiple secondary outlets cite the same single unverified source, creating an illusion of independent confirmation?
selfCheck.explanation: Circular reporting masquerades one unverified claim as multi-source corroboration.

selfCheck.prompt: How many genuinely independent primary sources are the baseline minimum for corroborating high-stakes claims?
selfCheck.explanation: At least two genuinely independent sources are required to establish baseline corroboration.

title: Lab 29: Conceptual Architecture of Surface, Deep, and Dark Web Telemetry
objective: Accurately classify web layers conceptually and evaluate safe clearnet CTI alternatives for monitoring ransomware/breach disclosures.
steps: Classify five examples into Surface Web, Deep Web, or Dark Web: (1) Public Wikipedia article, (2) Your private hospital patient portal over HTTPS, (3) Unlisted company intranet database, (4) Tor `.onion` hidden service mirror of a major newspaper (e.g., BBC/NYT onion mirror), (5) Public ICANN RDAP.
Review why corporate SOCs rely on vetted clearnet CTI feeds, MISP communities, and legal counsel rather than ad-hoc analyst browsing of criminal forums.
expectedOutcome: Conceptual classification table and enterprise legal safety policy for dark-web-related threat intelligence.

selfCheck.prompt: Is a password-protected university library or online banking portal on standard HTTPS part of the Deep Web or the Dark Web?
selfCheck.hint: Unindexed standard web behind login = ____ Web.
selfCheck.explanation: The Deep Web encompasses all unindexed/authenticated standard web pages; the Dark Web specifically requires overlay networks.

selfCheck.prompt: What top-level special-use domain suffix (RFC 7686) designates Tor hidden services (`._____`)?
selfCheck.explanation: RFC 7686 reserves `.onion` for anonymous onion-routed hidden services.

title: Lab 30: Writing an Admiralty-Graded BLUF Intelligence Report
objective: Synthesize multi-source OSINT findings into an executive BLUF brief with Admiralty source ratings, confidence levels, and ACH matrix.
steps: Assign Admiralty grades (`A1` through `F6`) to three pieces of evidence: (1) Official ICANN RDAP / CT log cryptographic record (`A1`), (2) Reputable CERT bulletin citing probable campaign link (`B2`), (3) Unverified paste-site claim with no technical corroboration (`F6`).
Draft a 4-sentence Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF) paragraph stating Key Judgment, Confidence Level (High/Moderate/Low), and Evidence Basis.
Export your report to Markdown or Google Docs for portfolio review.
expectedOutcome: Portfolio-grade Threat Intelligence Report ready for Stage B Final Certification.

selfCheck.prompt: In the Admiralty Code, what two-character grade represents a Completely Reliable source (`A`) with Confirmed information (`1`)?
selfCheck.explanation: A1 is the highest Admiralty rating: Completely reliable source + Independently confirmed information.

selfCheck.prompt: What four-letter acronym stands for placing your core conclusion in the very first paragraph of an intelligence report?
selfCheck.explanation: BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front) ensures busy decision-makers grasp the key judgment and confidence immediately.
